title: 2 Chronicles 12:13–16
context: Rehoboam strengthens himself in Jerusalem. He was forty-one when he began to reign and reigned seventeen years in the city the LORD chose, and his mother was Naamah the Ammonitess, as in 1 Kings 14:21. The Chronicler’s verdict is that he did evil, “because he didn’t set his heart to seek the LORD” (12:14). His acts are said to be written in the histories of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer, where 1 Kings 14:29 refers to the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. War with Jeroboam continues, and Abijah succeeds him; 1 Kings 14:31 gives the son’s name as Abijam. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: a heart that does not seek the LORD leads to evil, yet God keeps David’s line on the throne in the city he chose.

verses.text: So King Rehoboam strengthened himself in Jerusalem and reigned; for Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city which the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam strengthens himself in Jerusalem and reigns seventeen years, beginning at forty-one, in the city the LORD chose. His mother is Naamah the Ammonitess. Arminian readers note that God’s choice of Jerusalem gives Rehoboam both privilege and responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God keeps his promise to preserve a lamp for David in Jerusalem. The details match 1 Kings 14:21. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a regnal summary, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 14:21, and neither builds a contrast on the age or the length of the reign.

verses.text: He did that which was evil, because he didn’t set his heart to seek the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “He did that which was evil, because he didn’t set his heart to seek the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the Chronicler locates the problem in Rehoboam’s heart and its direction. His evil came from failing to seek God, a failure for which he was responsible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the root of Rehoboam’s failure in a heart not set on God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a key statement of the Chronicler’s theology, contrasting Rehoboam with those who set their hearts to seek the LORD (11:16), and both see seeking God as the heart of faithfulness.

verses.text: Now the acts of Rehoboam, first and last, aren’t they written in the histories of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer, in the genealogies? There were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam’s acts are written in the histories of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer, and there were continual wars with Jeroboam. Arminian readers note the Chronicler’s reference to prophetic records, which shows that the account rests on earlier sources.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the sources named, which differ from the source cited in 1 Kings 14:29. The continual war echoes 1 Kings 14:30. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a closing formula that points to fuller records and notes the ongoing conflict between the two kingdoms.

verses.text: Rehoboam slept with his fathers, and was buried in David’s city; and Abijah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam dies, is buried in David’s city, and Abijah his son reigns in his place. Arminian readers note that Rehoboam’s reign, marked by folly, humility, and failure, ends with the throne passing to the next generation. 1 Kings 14:31 names the son Abijam.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that despite Rehoboam’s failures, David’s line continues on the throne in Jerusalem. God keeps his promise to David even through unfaithful heirs. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuity under God’s covenant, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 14:31.
